What I ran: one job (01a160ad-7a8c-737e-9a1b-67f372933f9e) on garnet:mock with 6 circuits, 1000 shots each, for times 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. Each circuit starts the 6 spins as up, down, up, down, up, down. It then evolves them under the Heisenberg chain (J = 1, spin = Pauli/2) in Trotter steps of 0.2. Each step applies the bond gates on even bonds, then odd bonds. Each bond gate was compiled to 3 CZ gates, so the CZ count is 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 and 150. I read the CZ counts and measured qubits back from the payload the server received. Every circuit measures 6 qubits.

What a perfect quantum computer shows (noiseless simulation of the submitted circuits): Neel order is 1.00 at t=0, then 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.35, 0.38 at t=0.4 to 2.0. So the perfect up-down pattern melts quickly. Within about t=1.2 it falls to roughly 0.4 and then levels off around 0.35 to 0.4. That fits a small chain with an open end, where the order does not reach zero. Some of the remaining 0.35 is a finite-size effect and some is Trotter error.

What the test device gave back: -0.18, -0.41, -0.39, -0.40, -0.41, -0.41. These do not follow the physics. At t=0 the circuit only flips three qubits, so a perfect device returns 101010 with Neel order 1. The mock instead returned a spread of 000000, 111111 and a few repeating patterns in roughly equal shares (about 25% each). It does this for every circuit, whatever the circuit contains. The mock is a plumbing test of the job path, not a simulator, so its counts carry no physics. Only the noiseless simulation above is a valid reference. Real Garnet would also add noise. With 150 CZ gates at t=2 it would likely wash the signal toward zero.

What this says about KCuF3: neighbors want to point opposite ways, but the Heisenberg exchange also lets neighboring opposite spins swap places. Starting from a perfect alternating pattern, quantum motion spreads the pattern out in a short time (about 1 to 2 in units of 1/J). In the real crystal, this is why the spin chain has no ordinary frozen up-down order at low temperature. It shows a fluctuating quantum state instead. This is a 6-spin toy model, so it shows the trend, not material numbers. Job status: completed, billed_seconds 1.0 (mock, 0 credits).
